clue.text: Foreign aristocrat, one having a clearout?

definitions.meaning: a member of Prussia's landowning nobility, known by a German title meaning young lord
someone who throws out unwanted clutter, named by adding -er to a slang verb for discarding; the question mark flags the invented noun

explanation.surface: A nobleman from abroad is getting rid of his unwanted possessions.
explanation.walkthrough: Two definitions side by side: the comma separates a real German title from an invented noun for a person who junks things. Junkers were the landed gentry of Prussia.
explanation.definitionFit: Prussia's landed nobles bore this German title, and anyone who junks old clutter earns the same label by adding -er to the verb.

clue.text: Revolutionary sailor having lost foot — old wound

indicators.note: in a down entry a word's foot is its bottom letter, so the sailor loses his last letter

parts.note: jack, as in jack tar, is an old word for a sailor
O is the abbreviation for old, as in OT for Old Testament
a bite is a wound made by teeth

explanation.surface: A rebel seaman who had a leg amputated still carries the scar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having lost foot' removes the bottom letter of JACK in this down entry, leaving JAC. The Jacobites rose in 1715 and 1745 to put the exiled Stuarts back on the British throne.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose synonym: supporters of the exiled Stuart kings took up arms to overthrow Britain's Hanoverian monarchy, making them rebels against the state.

clue.text: Broad area, and no people

parts.note: nor continues a negative, meaning 'and not': 'no food nor drink' is 'no food and no drink'
folk are people in general

explanation.surface: A wide expanse of land without a single inhabitant.
explanation.walkthrough: The Broads are a network of shallow lakes and rivers in this English county, so 'Broad area' means the place they are found, not a wide space.
explanation.definitionFit: Punning description: the East Anglian county is home to the Broads, a famous network of navigable lakes and rivers.

clue.text: Antelope gambols around unknown, distant world

indicators.note: around means the rearranged letters go round the piece that follows
to gambol is to skip and frolic about, so the animal's letters jump into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
X is the usual algebraic symbol for an unknown quantity

explanation.surface: A gazelle frolics about in an unfamiliar, far-off land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gambols' rearranges ANTELOPE into EOPLANET, and 'around' wraps that round X, the unknown of algebra, which looks like an adjective for the world.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: a planet orbiting a star other than our Sun lies many light years from Earth.

clue.text: No information on the way? It makes us sick

indicators.note: in an across clue, one thing on another conventionally follows it, so the first two words come after the route

parts.note: a path is a way or route to somewhere
no as a quantity is zero, nought, which looks like the letter O
gen is British slang for information, as in 'give me the gen'

explanation.surface: Passengers complain that being told nothing about their journey leaves them fed up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' sends 'No information' to the back, after the way. O stands for no in the sense of zero, and GEN is British forces slang for information.
explanation.definitionFit: Description by effect: a disease-causing microbe such as a virus or bacterium is exactly what makes people ill.

clue.text: Customs investigator in heart of europol probing collector of gems

indicators.note: probing means the letters taken from the agency's name push into the collector

parts.note: an anthologist gathers choice poems or stories, literary gems, into one collection

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its centre, here the middle three letters

explanation.surface: A border-control detective at the centre of a European police inquiry looks into a jewel hoarder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Customs' are a people's traditions, not border checks. 'heart of' takes ROP from europol, and 'probing' pushes it into ANTHOLOGIST, whose gems are choice poems; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Punning description: a scholar of human societies studies their traditions, rituals and habits.

clue.text: Philosopher on what is coming up

indicators.note: in a down entry, coming up means the two pieces before it are read from the bottom upwards as one run

parts.note: in cricket the on side of the field is also called the leg side
eh? is the grunt of someone who did not catch a remark, meaning 'what?'

explanation.surface: A thinker holds forth on events that lie ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface has a thinker discussing the future. In cricket the 'on' side of the field is also called the LEG side, and 'is coming up' makes that plus a puzzled grunt for 'what' read upwards as one run.
explanation.definitionFit: Example of the category: the German idealist who devised the dialectic of thesis and antithesis was an influential thinker.

clue.text: Rock finally covered by onset of arctic ice

indicators.note: finally points at the rock's last letter, and covered by means another letter lies over it and takes its place

parts.note: granite is a hard igneous rock

indicators.note: the onset of something is its start, so take the opening letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: A crag at last disappears beneath the first of the polar sea-ice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally covered by' replaces the last letter of GRANITE with A, which 'onset of' takes from arctic. The ice is edible: a Sicilian dessert of flavoured crushed ice.
explanation.definitionFit: Example of the category: the Sicilian dessert of coarse, flavoured crushed ice is a frozen sweet.

clue.text: Upside-down on horse, exciting at first in infancy

indicators.note: in a down entry a word turned upside-down reads from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written, before it is turned over
a nag is an old or worn-out horse

indicators.note: at first asks for the opening letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: Dangling the wrong way up from a pony was a thrill, to begin with, for a small child.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upside-down' turns ON into NO and 'at first' takes the E of exciting; 'in' is a link. In law, infancy means being under the age of majority.
explanation.definitionFit: Legal synonym: both words name the period of being under age, a minor's years before full adulthood.

clue.text: Saucy girl and fraudulent miracle: her case comes up here?

parts.note: baggage is a dated word for a cheeky, impudent young woman

indicators.note: something fraudulent has been faked or doctored, so the letters of the next word are tampered with

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cheeky young woman faces a court hearing over a faked wonder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fraudulent' rearranges MIRACLE into RECLAIM; 'and' is a link. The 'case' is a suitcase rising onto the carousel at what British airports call baggage reclaim, not a court hearing.
explanation.definitionFit: Punning description: in an airport arrivals hall a traveller's suitcase rides up onto the carousel for collection.

clue.text: My angry outburst about second glutton

indicators.note: about means the two pieces before it sit round the piece that comes next

parts.note: my! and cor! are both British exclamations of surprise
a rant is a furious tirade
a mo is a moment, a second, as in 'half a mo'

explanation.surface: The speaker lost their temper over yet another greedy guest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' is an exclamation, matched by a British cry of surprise, and 'second' is a brief moment, not a placing. 'about' wraps the first two pieces, taken together, round the third.
explanation.definitionFit: Figurative sense: the seabird's voracious appetite for fish made its name a byword for a greedy person.

clue.text: Relative eating one seed

indicators.note: eating means the relative swallows the piece that follows, which ends up inside

parts.note: gran is the familiar British word for a grandmother
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A family member nibbles a single pip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eating' puts I, the Roman numeral one, inside GRAN, a grandmother.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a kernel of wheat, rice or barley is the seed of a cereal plant.

clue.text: Port good but not made legally

parts.note: Bootle is a dock town on the River Mersey beside Liverpool, in north-west England
G is a standard abbreviation for good, as on a grading scale

explanation.surface: The fortified wine tastes fine even though it was produced illicitly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' is a place, not a drink: Bootle is a docks town on the Mersey next to Liverpool. 'but' only joins the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Adjective sense: illicitly distilled liquor and pirated recordings are described with this word.

clue.text: Such stock can get you rich

definitions.meaning: railway carriages, wagons and locomotives are collectively called stock of this kind
slang for very wealthy, short for a phrase that ends 'in it' or 'in money'

explanation.surface: The right shares could make you a fortune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stock' suggests shares, but the first definition asks which word goes before stock to mean railway vehicles. 'can get you' merely links it to the second, a slang word for wealthy.
explanation.definitionFit: Railway carriages and wagons are collectively 'rolling stock', and someone 'rolling in it' is very wealthy, so one word serves both.

clue.text: South-east from London, almost without meaning it

parts.note: the phrase is a direction of travel, so it opens with the preposition of destination, 'to'

indicators.note: almost means the county's name stops just short, losing its final letter

parts.note: leave the capital in that direction and you reach the county of Kent, which fills England's south-east corner

explanation.surface: A traveller drifts out of the capital towards the coast, nearly by accident.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening is a direction of travel, not a synonym: go south-east from London and you are heading 'to' KENT, the county between the capital and the Channel. 'almost' drops its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Adjective use: a gesture or apology made only for show, as a formality, is offered insincerely.

clue.text: Get mad supporter on pitch to push a large right back

indicators.note: to push means shoving the two named letters along from where they sit in the word
right back says how far they are shoved: all the way to the very end

parts.note: a goalpost holds up the crossbar on a football pitch, so it is a support found there
taken as written
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: An enraged football fan runs onto the field to shove a burly defender.
explanation.walkthrough: A right back is a football defender, but here 'to push' and 'right back' shift A and L (large) from the middle of GOALPOST, the upright supporting the crossbar, to its end.
explanation.definitionFit: American slang idiom for flying into a violent rage, coined after shootings by US mail workers in the 1980s.

clue.text: Quickly holding hands, about to fail, but keep going

indicators.note: holding means the first word grips the assembled middle section inside it

parts.note: soon can mean promptly, as in 'as soon as possible'

indicators.note: about puts the two hands either side of the word for failing

parts.note: the left and right hands, abbreviated to L and R
an engine that dies has failed; to die is to stop working

explanation.surface: A couple hastily clasp hands, close to collapse, yet press on.
explanation.walkthrough: The hands are a left and a right, each shortened to its initial. 'about' sets them either side of the word for failing to make LDIER, which 'holding' puts inside the word for quickly; 'but' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: to persevere doggedly through hardship, as troops on a long march do.

clue.text: Hurry evenly and peacefully, without delay

indicators.note: evenly asks for the letters in the even positions of the word before it, the second and fourth

parts.note: to do something gently is to do it calmly, without force

explanation.surface: Make haste at a steady pace and calmly, wasting no time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'evenly' picks the second and fourth letters of Hurry, U and R, not a steady pace; 'and' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: something done with pressing haste is done immediately, at once.

clue.text: Type of poem of former time not written down

parts.note: the past is time gone by
an oral agreement or tradition is spoken, never put on paper

explanation.surface: A kind of verse from long ago that nobody ever committed to paper.
explanation.walkthrough: The second 'of' only links definition to wordplay; the surface runs the two pieces together as one ancient, unrecorded verse.
explanation.definitionFit: Genre name: verse idealising shepherds and country life, like Virgil's Eclogues, belongs to this literary kind.

clue.text: A boy dressed finally in rubber

parts.note: taken as written
a lad is a boy

indicators.note: finally asks for the last letter of the word before it

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A lad eventually got himself kitted out in latex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally' takes the D of dressed. The definition is not latex but someone who rubs: the Arabian Nights boy rubs a magic lamp to call up a genie.
explanation.definitionFit: Punning coinage: the Arabian Nights hero rubs a magic lamp to summon its genie, so he is one who rubs.

clue.text: King welcoming Henry and Franz?

indicators.note: welcoming means the king lets the next piece in, giving it room inside

parts.note: Lear is the king of Britain in Shakespeare's tragedy
H is the symbol for the henry, the SI unit of electrical inductance

explanation.surface: A monarch greets two guests, Henry and Franz.
explanation.walkthrough: 'welcoming' puts H inside LEAR, Shakespeare's king. 'Franz?' defines by example, the question mark admitting he is only one bearer of the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the Hungarian composer of the operetta The Merry Widow had this first name.

clue.text: Rejection of call for effort aboard

definitions.meaning: to give someone this is to sack them or end a relationship with them
the cry sailors raise as they haul together on a rope or anchor cable

explanation.surface: The crew of a ship refuse an appeal to work harder.
explanation.walkthrough: Two definitions joined by 'of': the informal noun for a dismissal, and the shout of sailors hauling together on a rope.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors shout it when hauling on a rope together, and informally to be given it is to be sacked or dumped.

clue.text: In car, let out, having travel sickness

indicators.note: In, at the head of the clue, says the rearranged word sits inside the car

parts.note: Jag is the familiar short name for a Jaguar, the British luxury car

indicators.note: out can mean astray or wrong, so the letters of the word before it are disordered

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A queasy passenger has to be allowed out of the vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a carsick passenger let out of a car, but the sickness is a flyer's. 'out' rearranges the word before it into ETL, and 'In' places that inside a British luxury car's nickname; 'having' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose description: the fatigue and disorientation after flying across time zones is a malaise brought on by a long journey.

clue.text: Fancy lace — it's used in knickers

definitions.note: a description standing in for a noun: understand 'it's' again as the subject, the stuff that is used there

indicators.note: fancy as an adjective means elaborately worked, so the letters after it are worked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
the apostrophe is dropped, leaving three letters

explanation.surface: Ornate trimming is a feature of ladies' underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' looks like a description of the lace but rearranges LACE and ITS. Knickers are women's underpants in British English, held up by a stretchy waistband.
explanation.definitionFit: Description by use: the stretchy rubber-threaded band in a waistband is what holds underwear up.

clue.text: Not using force, stealing a letter

indicators.note: not using means the word for stealing does without the abbreviation named next

parts.note: theft is the act of stealing
F is the physics symbol for force, as in F = ma
taken as written

explanation.surface: A thief pinches a piece of mail without resorting to violence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not using' removes F, the physics symbol for force, from THEFT to leave THET. The letter is a Greek character, not an item of post.
explanation.definitionFit: Example of the category: the eighth character of the Greek alphabet.

clue.text: Expression of serious expert

parts.note: grim means stern, grave or forbidding
an ace is someone who excels at something, as in a flying ace

explanation.surface: The look on the face of an earnest specialist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of' joins the definition to a two-part charade; the surface makes the whole thing read as one person's look.
explanation.definitionFit: Example of the category: a twisted look of pain or disgust is one thing a face can show.

clue.text: Say, pretty girl shortly back in small house

indicators.note: back means the two pieces before it are read from right to left as one run

parts.note: say introduces an example, just as e.g. (for example) does

indicators.note: shortly cuts the slang word short, removing its last letter

parts.note: doll is dated slang for an attractive young woman

explanation.surface: Someone calls out to an attractive young woman who will soon be home again in her cottage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' is not a hail but the usual flag for an example. 'shortly' trims the slang for a pretty girl to DOL, and 'back' turns both pieces round as one run; 'in' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a gatekeeper's cottage at the entrance to an estate, or a hunting cabin, is a modest dwelling.

clue.text: Off circling the earth, taking it all in?

indicators.note: circling means the first word goes round the next piece, like a satellite in orbit

parts.note: someone off work or off school is absent
an orb is a globe or sphere, a poetic word for a heavenly body such as our planet

explanation.surface: An astronaut away in orbit gazes down, drinking in the whole view.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition reads like sightseeing from space, but it describes what a sponge does with liquid; the question mark flags that play on 'taking it all in'. 'circling' wraps the word for off round the poetic globe.
explanation.definitionFit: Punning description: a sponge or blotting paper soaks up every drop of liquid it touches.

clue.text: Aim gun in outskirts of Grenoble? One might

definitions.note: the pronoun stands for the answer: a person who might well do what the rest of the clue describes

indicators.note: in places the first two pieces between the letters taken from the city's name
the outskirts of a town are its edges, so take the first and last letters of the city's name

parts.note: an end is a goal or purpose, as in 'to this end'
an arm is a weapon, as in firearm or small arms

explanation.surface: Somebody could be pointing a weapon on the fringes of a French Alpine city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outskirts of' takes G and E from Grenoble, and 'in' sets the words for aim and gun between them. 'One might' then refers to the whole scene, which fits an armed French policeman.
explanation.definitionFit: Allusive: French military police officers carry firearms, so one of them could do exactly this on the edge of a French city.

clue.text: Dog, almost twelve, collected by agent

indicators.note: collected by means the agent gathers up the shortened word and holds it inside

parts.note: a spy is a secret agent

indicators.note: almost stops the word for twelve one letter before its end

parts.note: noon is twelve o'clock in the day

explanation.surface: An elderly pet, nearly twelve years old, is picked up by a representative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'twelve' is a time of day, not the dog's age: 'almost' trims it to NOO, and 'collected by' places that inside the secret agent.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Charlie Brown's pet beagle in the Peanuts comic strip is a famous cartoon hound.
